body:
## Module 6 in two minutes

Every module so far has been about your own work. **This one is about the fact that the other side of the table got the same tools, at the same time, and used them faster.**

Three things changed about inbound complaints, and only two are problems.

**Length.** Two pages became **eight to twelve**, sometimes far more, not padding, but headings, numbered paragraphs, statutory references, recited context.

**Register.** The document reads as though a professional drafted it. And critically: **the correlation between an articulate document and an articulate, advised or well-resourced complainant has been severed**, which matters because a great deal of informal HR triage ran on exactly that correlation without anyone admitting it.

**Substance**, which is where it gets difficult. The grasp of the law may be thin even where the citations are correct. Asked to make a complaint sound serious, a model reaches for the vocabulary available (*bullying, harassment, discrimination, victimisation*) so minor incidents arrive dressed in protected-characteristic language. Not dishonesty. Register.

Two consequences. **Your obligation per matter did not change**: twelve pages containing three investigable allegations needs the same investigation as two pages containing three, plus two hours of reading. And **the escalated framing is now on the record** — once the document alleges discrimination, your response must address discrimination, even where the facts describe something else. You cannot decline the framing on the grounds that you think the model chose it.

### The rule, and the trap inside it

> **You judge the content, not the tool.**

Declining, downgrading, delaying or deprioritising a complaint **because it appears AI-generated** is itself actionable. **In the UK** (where the clearest guidance sits) refusing to process a grievance on that basis risks breaching the Acas Code, and where the complaint concerns discrimination, adverse treatment for raising it can amount to **victimisation** under the Equality Act 2010. **In the US** the analogue is retaliation exposure, plus the destruction of the prompt-and-appropriate-corrective-action posture your defence depends on. *We did not investigate promptly because the complaint appeared machine-written* is not a sentence anybody wants to advance. Same rule in both places; different citation. Take the specifics to your counsel.

Then the part that feels like the safe option and isn't:

> **Treating an AI-drafted submission with extra scepticism is the same error as treating it with extra deference.**

Both substitute a judgment about provenance for a judgment about content, and both leave a trace: in your notes, your triage record, the tone of your acknowledgement.

**So: do not record, and do not discuss, your view that a submission was AI-drafted.** Not because the observation is wrong, but because it is irrelevant to every decision you are about to make. And note the harder version — **a provenance judgment does not stop being one because the word is left out.** *"The statutory characterisations do not appear to reflect independent legal advice"* is the same decision in better clothes.

**The method, which is how you operate the rule at volume.**

A long submission is typically **a small number of factual allegations wrapped in a large amount of characterization, context and legal framing.** Fourteen pages might contain four things that happened. And:

> **Only the allegations generate an investigative obligation. The argument does not.**

The argument gets *acknowledged and addressed*: a writing task. The allegations get *investigated*: the expensive thing. Conflating them is what turns a fourteen-page document into a fourteen-page investigation, and it is why volume feels like it overwhelmed capacity when what changed is the ratio.

**1 · Extract the allegations as a numbered list** — assertion, where it appears, whether a date and other parties are named. **A permitted rung-one/two AI use**, verifiable by reading the document. **2 · Separate the framing**, which gets answered in your response. **3 · A human confirms the list**, checking two failures: a missed allegation, and **two allegations collapsed into one**: the one people miss, because the list looks complete. **4 · Send the numbered list back to the complainant.** *These are the matters I have understood you to raise and will investigate.* **Ten minutes, and the highest-value step in the module**. It corrects your extraction before you build on it, evidences engagement with the whole submission, and forecloses the argument that you investigated a narrower version.

**The forbidden step is the tempting one: a model may not decide which allegations are serious, in scope, or worth investigating.** That is the triage determination (rung five in rung-one clothing) and a manager agreeing with the classification afterwards is reviewing a conclusion, not making a decision.

**And the volume trap runs in reverse here: production got cheaper for the other side, and your obligation per matter did not change.** The answer is not reading faster. It is not paying investigative attention to argument.

**The full module adds two counterparties beyond the individual complainant.**

**The union.** Its right to information is a **statutory entitlement**, not a courtesy, and AI is now being applied to contract analysis, costing, and comparator research across employers. Which means **the information asymmetry that used to favour the employer is closing.** Your advantage was largely a *processing* advantage, and processing is what became cheap: a representative can now analyse the agreement you both signed more thoroughly than the person who negotiated it remembers doing. Two consequences, your information response will be analysed rather than filed, and requests may increasingly ask about **the systems you have deployed**, which you should not be answering for the first time in a live grievance.

**And the forum with no detection.** Fabricated citations are a documented problem in litigation, in three flavours: **entirely fictitious cases; fabricated citations to real cases; and real quotations from real cases that do not support (or contradict) the proposition they are cited for.** The third is hardest to catch because everything about it looks correct. The arbitration-specific finding:

> **In arbitration these failures appear and are largely neither reported nor sanctioned, because most arbitrators have no law clerks, no case-law database, and limited power to sanction.**

Read that as an operational fact, not an invitation. **Verify every citation in anything you file, by a person** — not because you will be sanctioned, but because you probably won't be, and the citation becomes part of a record that is wrong. **Check the other side's**, which is now a thing to do rather than assume. And understand the third edge: past practice and prior awards are the substance of contract interpretation, so **a forum with no detection is a forum where a fabricated authority can enter the precedent conversation and stay there.**
